text.p: Earnings estimates were slashed and the share price of ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG continued to tumble on Friday following the company's disappointing 1996 result and sober forecast for the current year.
Analysts, who admitted they had been overly optimistic about ABB's prospects and turned a deaf ear to the company's warnings, cut 1997 and 1998 profit forecasts by five to 20 percent.
"Expectations were too optimistic," said Otto Lehmann of Rotschild Bank AG late Thursday after attending a briefing on the 1996 results with ABB top executives.
"We can't blame the company," added Thomas Pfyl of Bank Vontobel.

Despite the reduction in earnings forecasts, analysts remain bullish about ABB's prospects and expect its shares to rebound later in the year as Europe's long-awaited recovery takes hold and the market's attention turns to 1998 earnings.
On Thursday ABB disappointed markets and analysts by reporting lower-than-expected 1996 results.

ABB's reported group net profit fell 6.2 percent to $1.233 billion from 1995. However, the 1995 result was inflated by a one-off payment of $250 million from Daimler-Benz AG in connection with a transportation venture.
Excluding this gain, ABB's 1996 group net profit rose 15.8 percent, a result ABB said was in line with its target.
But not only was the result a disappointment to the market, but ABB's forecast for 1997 was even more disappointing.
ABB forecast that its 1997 result would "reach at least the same level as in 1996."

Credit Suisse First Boston, one of the many securities houses to cut forecasts, said prior to Thursday's result the consensus was that the earnings of ABB's Swiss parent, ABB AG, would rise 24 percent.
"Obviously there is a large gap between market expectations and ABB's view," CSFB said.
During 1996 ABB had frequently warned about 1996, especially earnings at the Power Generation segment.
But analysts had widely underestimated the sharp 39 percent fall in the 1996 operating earnings of ABB's power generation.
Although the power generation segment is only ABB's second largest business segment, it has traditionally had the highest profit margin despite years of downward price pressure.
In 1996, however, the profit margin in power generation tumbled to 5.8 percent in 1996 from 8.9 percent.
ABB has already taken measures to address the segment's problems but the payoff will first come in 1998.

Armin Meyer, responsible for the power generation segment, told the news conference that 1996 was a year of investment to change the segment's production structures and move toward single global sourcing, which would reduce costs.
"1997 will be a year of consolidation and in 1998 we will have the full impact of the measures," Meyer said.
Another surprise was a 36 percent fall in ABB's fourth quarter net profit, traditionally ABB's strongest quarter.
At the news conference ABB's new chief executive and president Goran Lindahl had no specific explanation for the drop in the fourth quarter, apart from general business weakness.
"The weak fourth quarter reinforces the message of a weakening through 1996 and we don't see strong growth in 1997," Lindahl said.
On Friday shares of ABB's two quoted parent companies, Sweden's ABB AB and Switzerland's ABB AG, continued a fall that started on Thursday when ABB released its disappointing results.

Since ABB released its results early on Thursday, the A-shares of its Swedish parent ABB AB have lost 6.6 percent in Stockholm and in Zurich the bearer shares of the Swiss parent ABB AG have lost 7.4 percent.

The market's reaction is remarkably similar to that of exactly 12 months ago, when ABB's vague profit forecast at its 1996 news conference also surprised the market, leading to a followed by a swift, but temporary drop in its shares.
But ABB's shares have not only fallen victim to optimistic earnings forecasts, but also the "irrational exuberance" that has enveloped equity markets, including the Swiss.
"The market has become overheated," said Peter Gachnang of Bank Julius Baer.
Since the beginning of this year, the broad SPI index has risen 31 percent.
